newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rejects airdrop plan for refugees.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rejects airdrop plan for refugees.

text.p: Zaire rejected on Thursday a Canadian plan to air-drop food for thousands of refugees and Zaireans fleeing fighting in the east of the country.
"The Zairean government is categorically opposed to the Canadian proposition to drop foodstuffs for refugees and displaced Zaireans," Information Minister Boguo Makeli said in Kinshasa.
Canada, exasperated by the foot-dragging of its partners in an international humanitarian mission for eastern Zaire, suggested this week that air-drops of food could be made.
Boguo said Zaire was worried about the safety of such airdrops and the fact that they would be staged from neighbouring countries it accuses of aggression.

Aid agencies estimated that there were 1.2 million refugees in eastern Zaire before the mass return in mid-November, prompted by fighting in the area between the rebels, Zairean troops and Rwandan Hutu extremists in the refugee camps.
The U.S. military believes 600,000 have returned to Rwanda, mostly from the camps around Goma, but opinions differ on how many refugees remain in eastern Zaire.
Aid workers had to leave because of the fighting in October and have only in recent days been allowed back by the rebels to begin assessment work.

Refugees who were in camps to the south of Goma, in the region of Bukavu on the southern shore of Lake Kivu, have been hard to trace. Aid workers reported only a trickle of refugees across the border to Rwanda from Bukavu on Thursday.

Refugees crossing at Bukavu said they believed that a group of at least 100,000 Rwandan refugees was being driven by Interahamwe militiamen towards Walikale, about 50 km (30 miles) west of the Bukavu-Goma road.

The Hutu Interahamwe and troops of the former Rwandan army took part in the genocide of up to one million Rwandan Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994. A Tutsi army subsequently overran the country, and Hutus fled into Zaire.
Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, the Canadian commander of the proposed intervention force for eastern Zaire, travelled to the rebel-held city of Goma on Thursday.
Baril crossed the border from Rwanda in a three-vehicle convoy and went directly to the palace in Goma of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko. The palace is now in rebel hands.
Baril declined to speak to journalists as he crossed the border from Rwanda and again refused all comment after leaving the palace.

Aides refused to say whether he had met rebel leader Laurent Kabila as planned, and, in farcical scenes, tried to prevent carloads of journalists following when Baril drove off towards nearby Sake. They were finally stopped on the road to Minova.
Baril's aides said he would hold a news conference later on Thursday when he returned to the border.
On Wednesday, in the Rwandan capital Kigali, Baril said be would be going to Zaire to seek more information on the location and condition of refugees remaining in east Zaire.

"That's what we are trying to find out and we're putting every means that we have -- very sophisticated right down to little old me, who is going to take a look at it tomorrow," he told reporters after a meeting with Rwandan Vice-President Paul Kagame, seen as the strongman of the Rwandan regime.
The Rwandan government says any multinational force for Zaire is irrelevant as most Rwandan refugees have gone home. It wants aid to go to the returnees.

Officials of the United Nations UNHCR refugee agency were scheduled to be present at the talks on Thursday with Kabila, who, like his backers in Kigali, is hostile to the arrival of any multinational force.
